parts.title: Swimming lessons enquiry
parts.desc: A telephone conversation between a man and a receptionist at a leisure centre.

script.t: Part 1. You will hear a telephone conversation between a man and a receptionist at a leisure centre. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.
Good morning, Riverside Leisure Centre, Emma speaking. How can I help?
Oh, hello. I'm calling about swimming lessons for my son. I saw a leaflet about the autumn courses.
Of course. Let me just take a few details. What's your son's name?
It's Leo. Leo Hartley.
Could you spell the surname for me, please?
Yes, it's H, A, R, T, L, E, Y.
Thank you. And how old is Leo?
He's eight. He turned eight in July.
Lovely. Can he swim already? We put children into groups depending on how far they can swim without stopping.
He can do about ten metres. Actually, no, sorry, he swam twenty-five metres on holiday last month. He was very proud of himself.
Twenty-five metres, that's great. That puts him in our Stage Three group. Stage Three runs on Wednesdays after school, and on Saturdays.
Wednesdays would be ideal, actually.
I'm afraid the Wednesday group is already full this term. There's still space on Saturday, though.
Oh, that's a shame. Well, Saturday it is, then.
There are two Saturday sessions: one at nine fifteen and one at ten fifteen.
Nine fifteen is a bit early for us. He has football first thing. The later one, please.
Ten fifteen, then. I'll put him down for that. His teacher will be Ms Okafor. That's O, K, A, F, O, R. She's been teaching here for years, and the children love her.
Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.
Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.
Is there anything he needs to bring?
Towels are provided in the changing rooms, so he only needs his swimming costume, a swimming hat, and goggles.
Right. And how much is the course?
It's ten weeks, and the price is sixty-eight pounds for the whole course.
Is there any discount available?
Yes, if a parent has a fitness membership with us, you get ten per cent off.
I don't, unfortunately. Maybe I should think about it.
Could I take your address for the booking?
Yes, it's thirty-one Mill Lane, Caversham.
And the postcode?
R G 4, 7 T N.

R G 4, 7 T N. Thank you. Now, the first lesson would normally be on Saturday the thirteenth of September, but the pool is closed that day for maintenance, so the course will start the following Saturday, the twentieth.
The twentieth. Perfect. Thank you very much.
You're welcome. Goodbye.
That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Hillside Community Garden
parts.desc: A volunteer coordinator welcomes new volunteers to a community garden.

script.t: Part 2. You will hear a man talking to a group of new volunteers at a community garden. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Hillside Community Garden. My name's Tom, and I coordinate the volunteers here. Before we start work, I'd like to tell you a little about the garden and how things are organised.

The garden was created eleven years ago on land that used to be the car park of the old hospital. When the hospital moved to its new site, a group of local residents persuaded the council to let them turn the land into a garden, rather than sell it for housing. In the first year, everything had to be grown in raised beds, because the soil under the car park was too poor to use. These days we've improved a lot of the ground, but we still use the raised beds for vegetables.

We have around sixty volunteers in total, but most people come once a week or less, so on a typical day there are about fifteen of us here. You don't need any experience. Many of our volunteers had never grown anything before they joined. What we do ask is that you sign in at the shed when you arrive, so we always know who's on site.

Now, a few practical points. We're open to volunteers on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays, from nine until one. Lunch isn't provided, but there's a kettle in the shed, and on the last Saturday of each month we all bring some food to share. Gloves and tools are provided. The only thing we ask you to bring is suitable footwear: boots or strong shoes, not trainers, please, as the paths can get very muddy.

Some of you have asked about taking produce home. The rule is simple. Volunteers are welcome to take a share of whatever's ready, but most of the vegetables go to the food bank in the town centre, which collects every Saturday afternoon.
Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

Right, let me tell you about the different areas of the garden. If you look at the plan in your welcome pack, you'll see the orchard at the top of the slope. It has twenty fruit trees, and it's the oldest part of the garden. It's also where we hold our open day every September.
Next to it is the wildlife area, which we leave fairly wild on purpose. There's a pond there that was dug by children from the local primary school, so please be careful near the edge.
The greenhouse is the place to be in winter. It's heated, and it's where we start off all our seedlings in early spring before they go out into the beds.

Down by the main gate you'll find the sensory garden, which was designed for residents of the care home next door. The plants there were chosen for their smell and their texture, so please don't cut anything back without asking first.
And finally, behind the shed, there's the compost area, where all our garden waste is recycled. That's also where we keep the bee hives, so it's best to stay calm and move slowly if you go near them.
That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Food waste project
parts.desc: Two students, Maya and Sam, discuss their research project with their tutor.

script.t: Part 3. You will hear two students, Maya and Sam, talking to their tutor about a research project on food waste. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.
Come in, both of you. So, you wanted to talk about your project on food waste in the university canteens.
Yes. We've finished collecting our data, and we'd like some advice before we start writing it up.
Good. Remind me how you collected the data.

We weighed the food left on plates in the main canteen at lunchtime over two weeks. We'd originally planned to do it at both lunch and dinner, but the canteen manager asked us not to come in the evenings because it would get in the way of the staff, so we stuck to lunch.
That's fine, as long as you explain it in your methods. What were the main findings?
The surprising thing was that it wasn't the main dishes that were wasted most. It was the side dishes, especially the salad and the bread that came automatically with every meal.
Yes, we'd expected the hot meals to be the problem, because the portions are quite big. But in fact people mostly finished those.
Interesting. Did you talk to any of the students?

We handed out a short questionnaire, and we got a hundred and twenty responses, which was more than we'd hoped for. The most common reason people gave for leaving food wasn't that they didn't like it. It was that they simply hadn't asked for it. It just came on the plate.
That's a useful point for your recommendations. What are you planning to suggest?

We thought about recommending smaller plates, because there's research showing that works in restaurants. But given what students told us, we think the most effective change would be to let people choose whether they want bread and salad, instead of serving them automatically.
That makes sense. It follows directly from your evidence.
Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.
Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
Now, let's talk about the structure of the report. How long is your literature review at the moment?
About two thousand words.
That's too long for a report of this size. I'd cut it to about half that, and keep only the studies that are directly relevant to universities.
OK. What about the methods section? It's quite short at the moment.

Short is fine for methods, but you need to say more about how you actually weighed the waste: what equipment you used, and how you separated the different types of food. Someone else should be able to repeat your study.
Right. And in the results, we've got lots of tables with the daily figures.
Put the full daily tables in an appendix, and just include a summary chart in the results section itself.
And the discussion?
I read your draft of the discussion, and honestly, I wouldn't change much. It's clear and well argued. Leave it as it is.
Great. And the conclusion?
The conclusion needs a short paragraph on the limitations of the study. For example, that you only looked at lunch, and only in one canteen.
That's a good point. Thank you.
That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

The canteen manager asked them to.
They did not have enough time.

parts.title: How honeybees communicate
parts.desc: A lecture about the dance language of honeybees.

script.t: Part 4. You will hear part of a lecture about how honeybees communicate. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
Good afternoon. Today I'm going to talk about one of the most remarkable systems of communication in the animal world: the way honeybees tell each other where to find food.

The person most associated with this research is the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who began studying bees in the early twentieth century. Von Frisch noticed that when a single bee found a good source of food, such as a dish of sugar water he had placed in a field, large numbers of other bees from the same hive soon arrived. But the first bee did not lead them there. Somehow, information was being passed on inside the hive.

To find out how, von Frisch used hives with glass walls, so that he could watch the bees' behaviour, and he marked individual bees with small dots of paint so that he could follow them. He observed that a bee returning with food performed movements on the surface of the honeycomb, which he called dances. In 1973, he shared the Nobel Prize for this work.

Von Frisch described two main types of dance. When food is close to the hive, within about fifty metres, the bee performs what he called the round dance, moving in small circles. This tells the other bees that food is nearby, but it doesn't tell them in which direction. So they search around the hive, using the scent of the flowers carried on the dancer's body to help them.

When the food is further away, the bee performs the waggle dance. Here, the bee runs in a straight line while shaking its body from side to side, then loops back and repeats the movement. Two pieces of information are contained in this dance.

First, direction. Inside the dark hive, the bee dances on a vertical surface, and the angle of the straight run, compared with vertically upwards, represents the angle between the food and the position of the sun. So if the bee runs straight up the comb, the food is in the same direction as the sun.

Second, distance. The longer the waggle run lasts, the further away the food is. Researchers have found that each second of waggling corresponds to roughly a kilometre of flight, although this varies between populations of bees. And because the sun moves across the sky during the day, the bees also adjust the angle of their dance over time. Remarkably, they do this even when they have been inside the hive for a while.

For many years, some scientists doubted that the dance really carried information. They argued that bees might simply be following smells. The question was settled in the early two thousands by experiments using radar, which tracked individual bees as they left the hive after watching a dance. The results showed that the bees flew directly towards the area indicated by the dance.

Today, the waggle dance is not only of interest to biologists. Engineers have used it as a model for computer programs that share tasks between many simple units. And beekeepers can learn about the health of their colonies by watching the dances. If bees are travelling very long distances, for instance, it may mean that there are few flowers nearby.
That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
That is the end of the listening test.

Hello, I'd like to book a room for a company meeting next month, please.
Certainly. Could I have your name first?
Yes, it's Irina Petrova. That's P, E, T, R, O, V, A.

parts.title: The city bike-share scheme
parts.desc: A local radio presenter explains a new bike-share scheme.

script.t: Part 2. You will hear a radio presenter talking about a new bike-share scheme in a city. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.
Good morning, and welcome to City Matters. This week, the new bike-share scheme finally opens to the public, so I'm going to tell you how it works and answer some of the questions you've sent in.

The scheme was originally planned to start in the spring, but it was delayed when the company building the docking stations went out of business, and the council had to find a new supplier. The good news is that the delay gave them time to add more bikes. There will now be six hundred bikes at launch, instead of the four hundred first announced, and around half of them are electric.

Many of you have asked whether you need a smartphone. You don't. The easiest way to hire a bike is through the app, but you can also buy a card at any library or at the main bus station, and use that at the docking stations.

As for prices, the first thirty minutes of every journey are free if you have an annual membership, which costs sixty pounds. If you don't want to join, you can pay as you go: it's one pound to unlock a bike, and then ten pence a minute. Electric bikes cost a little more, but the scheme is still cheaper than a taxi for most journeys in the centre.
One important rule: bikes must be returned to a docking station. If you leave a bike anywhere else, you'll be charged a fee of twenty pounds.
Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

Now, let me tell you about some of the docking stations. The largest one is at the railway station, with space for eighty bikes. It's expected to be the busiest, so the operators will check it every two hours to make sure there are always bikes available.

At the university, the docking station is next to the library rather than the main entrance, because the entrance is on a steep hill. The station at Riverside Park has been placed close to the cafe, and that's the only one where you'll find a pump and basic tools for repairs.

The station on Market Square is a little unusual: it's only open from six in the morning until midnight, because the square is closed to all traffic at night. And finally, the new station at the hospital has been reserved, during the first month, for hospital staff only, as a trial. If it works well, it will open to everyone in the new year.
That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Presentation on island energy
parts.desc: Two students, Leila and Ben, plan a presentation with their tutor.

script.t: Part 3. You will hear two students, Leila and Ben, discussing their presentation with their tutor. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.
So, your presentation is on renewable energy for small island communities. How are you getting on?
Quite well. We've decided to focus on one island in Scotland and one in the Pacific, so we can compare them.
Why those two?
We wanted islands of a similar size, so that the comparison would be fair. And there's good data available for both, which wasn't true for some of the others we looked at.
Good reasoning. What have you found so far?

The biggest surprise for me was the cost. I'd assumed that solar and wind would be cheaper on the mainland, but on both islands they turned out to be cheaper than the diesel they used before, because importing fuel by boat is so expensive.
And what I found interesting was that on the Scottish island, the community owns the wind turbines themselves. The profits go into a local fund.
What is that fund used for?
Mostly for insulating people's homes, so that they use less energy in the first place. They've also helped to pay for an electric minibus.
And the Pacific island?

There, the main problem is storage. Solar power works well during the day, but they need batteries for the evenings, and the batteries don't last long in the heat and humidity. That's the main challenge they're working on now.
Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.
Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
Now, let's think about how you'll organise the presentation. You have twenty minutes. Who's doing what?
I thought I'd start with the introduction and background, and then Ben would present the two case studies.
That's fine, but I'd suggest you each present one case study. Otherwise the audience hears one voice for too long.
Good idea. Then I'll do the Pacific island and Leila can do Scotland.
What about visuals?
We've got a lot of graphs of energy production. Maybe too many.

I'd choose just one graph for each island, the clearest one, and put the rest in a handout. For the introduction, a map would be more useful than a graph, so the audience can see where the islands are.
And for the conclusion?
For the conclusion, rather than repeating your findings, end with a question for the audience to discuss. That always works well in this class.
And what about the questions at the end?
Allow five minutes for questions, and prepare answers in advance for the obvious ones, especially about cost. Someone always asks about cost.
That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Maps and the shape of the world

script.t: Part 4. You will hear part of a lecture about how maps show the world. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
Good morning. Today I want to look at a problem that every map maker faces: how do you show the surface of a sphere, the Earth, on a flat piece of paper or a screen?

The short answer is that you can't do it perfectly. If you've ever tried to flatten the peel of an orange, you'll know that it tears or stretches. In the same way, every flat map must distort something: the shapes of countries, their sizes, the distances between places, or the directions between them. The method used to transfer the globe onto a flat surface is called a projection, and each projection makes a different choice about what to keep accurate and what to sacrifice.

The most famous projection was created in 1569 by the Flemish map maker Gerardus Mercator. His map was designed for sailors. On it, a line of constant compass direction appears as a straight line, which made it much easier to plan a route across the ocean. That was a huge advantage at the time, and the Mercator projection became the standard for navigation.

The cost of this accuracy in direction is a distortion of size. On a Mercator map, areas far from the equator appear much larger than they really are. Greenland, for example, looks roughly the same size as Africa, when in fact Africa is about fourteen times larger. Countries near the poles, such as Canada and Russia, also appear enormous.

In the twentieth century, some critics argued that the Mercator map, which was widely used in schools, gave a misleading picture of the world. In the nineteen seventies, the German historian Arno Peters promoted an alternative: an equal-area projection, in which every country is shown at its correct relative size. The price is that shapes are stretched, so that Africa and South America look long and thin. His map was popular with some charities and teachers, though many map makers criticised it.

Today, many atlases use compromise projections, which don't keep any single property perfectly accurate but keep all the distortions fairly small. One well-known example is the Robinson projection, which was adopted for world maps by the National Geographic Society for about ten years.

Interestingly, the digital maps on our phones use a version of Mercator's projection. The reason is practical: when you zoom in on a small area, such as a city street, Mercator keeps the angles correct, so that streets that meet at right angles still appear to meet at right angles. At that scale, the distortion of size doesn't matter. So a sixteenth-century solution for sailors is still guiding us around our cities today.
That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
That is the end of the listening test.

Lost property office, how can I help you?
Hi. I left a bag on a train yesterday evening, and I wondered if anyone has handed it in.
I'll take some details and check. Which train were you on?
It was the six forty from Bristol. I got off here at about eight o'clock.
Six forty from Bristol. And what kind of bag is it?
It's a backpack. A dark green backpack, quite large, with a red stripe on the front.
Can you tell me what was inside?
My laptop, mainly. Oh, and a book and an umbrella. And a jacket. No, sorry, the jacket I had with me. Just the laptop, the book and the umbrella.
Was there anything with your name on it?
Yes, the laptop has a label with my surname and my phone number on it.
Could I have your name, please?
It's Daniel Collins. Collins with two Ls.
And do you remember where you were sitting on the train?
In coach C, I think. Yes, coach C, near the door.
Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

Right, Mr Collins, I've checked our records, and a green backpack was handed in last night by one of the cleaning staff. It sounds like yours.
Oh, that's brilliant. Can I collect it today?
Yes, the office is open until half past six. You'll need to bring some photo identification, such as a passport or driving licence.
No problem. Is there any charge?
There's a standard handling fee of three pounds fifty for items over a certain value. Laptops are included.
That's fine. Where exactly is the office?
We're on platform one, next to the ticket office. If you come through the main entrance, turn left, and we're just past the cafe.
And could I give you my phone number, in case there's a problem?
Yes, please.
It's oh seven seven, double four, nine three one, five eight two.
Oh seven seven, four four, nine three one, five eight two. Thank you. Your reference number is L K two three nine. Please quote that when you arrive.
L K two three nine. Thank you so much.

parts.title: A tour of Ashcombe House
parts.desc: A guide welcomes visitors to a historic country house.

script.t: Part 2. You will hear a guide talking to visitors at a historic house. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Ashcombe House. I'm Helen, and I'll be your guide this morning. Before we go in, let me give you a little background and a few practical points.

The house was built in the seventeen nineties for a family who had made their fortune in the wool trade. It stayed in the same family for almost two hundred years, until the last owner, who had no children, left it to a heritage charity in nineteen seventy-eight. Since then it's been open to the public every summer.

Most of the house is as the family left it, but one thing has changed recently. Last year, we reopened the kitchen, which had been closed for repairs after a flood, and it's now one of the most popular rooms on the tour.

Our tour takes about an hour. Photography is allowed in most rooms, but please don't use flash anywhere, as it damages the paintings and fabrics. There's no photography at all in the library, because some of the books there are on loan from a private collection.
After the tour, you're welcome to explore the gardens on your own. The tea room is open until five, and your ticket also gives you a ten per cent discount in the gift shop.
Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

Now, if you look at the plan in your leaflet, I'll tell you about the rooms we'll be visiting. We'll start in the entrance hall, which has the most impressive ceiling in the house. It was painted by an Italian artist and took three years to complete.
From there we go into the dining room. The table is set exactly as it would have been for a dinner party in eighteen-twenty, using the family's original silver.
Next is the library, where you can see the desk at which one of the family's daughters wrote her novels. She published four books under a man's name, which was common for women writers at that time.
Then we'll go downstairs to the kitchen, which I mentioned earlier. Children especially enjoy it, because they're allowed to try grinding spices and making butter.
And we finish in the music room, which is the only room that is still used for its original purpose: we hold concerts there on the first Sunday of every month.
That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Survey on student part-time jobs
parts.desc: Two students, Aisha and Tom, discuss their survey with their tutor.

script.t: Part 3. You will hear two students, Aisha and Tom, talking to their tutor about a survey they carried out. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.
Hello, Aisha, Tom. You've finished your survey on part-time work, I hear.
Yes, we sent the questionnaire to all the first-year students in our department, and about forty per cent replied.
That's a reasonable response rate. How did you get people to reply?
We tried email first, but very few people answered. What really worked was asking lecturers to give us five minutes at the start of a lecture, so students could fill it in on their phones.
Clever. And the results?

Just over half the students who replied have a part-time job. The most common type of work is in shops and cafes, which we expected. But we didn't expect so many students to be tutoring school children. That was the second most common job.
Interesting. Why do you think that is?
Students told us it pays better than shop work and the hours are flexible. You can do it in the evening, after lectures.
What about the effects on their studies?

That was the most complicated part. Students who worked up to ten hours a week said it didn't affect their studies at all. Some even said it helped them organise their time better. But for those working more than fifteen hours, most said they had missed lectures or handed in work late.
So the number of hours seems to be the key factor.
Exactly. And most of the students working long hours said they did it because of the cost of rent, not for extra spending money.
Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.
Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
Now, about writing it up. You need to think about the limitations of your study.
Well, the sample was only from one department.
Yes, that's the main one. Mention it in the introduction as well as the conclusion, so readers know from the start.
What about the charts? We have quite a few.
Use a bar chart for the types of jobs, it's much clearer than the pie chart you have now. And for the hours worked, a simple table would be fine.
Should we include the students' comments?
Definitely. Choose four or five short quotations that illustrate your main points. They make the report much more vivid. But don't include any names.
And the recommendations?

Keep them practical. For example, you could suggest that the university advertises more on-campus jobs, which are usually more flexible about exam periods. And I'd send a short summary of your findings to the student union. They'll be interested.
That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Coral reefs
parts.desc: A lecture about coral reefs and how they are changing.

script.t: Part 4. You will hear part of a lecture about coral reefs. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
Today's lecture is about coral reefs, which are among the most diverse and also the most threatened ecosystems on the planet.

Let's start with a basic question: what is coral? Many people assume it's a plant or a rock, but in fact corals are animals. A coral reef is built by tiny creatures called polyps, each only a few millimetres across, which live together in huge colonies. Each polyp produces a hard skeleton of calcium carbonate, essentially limestone, and over thousands of years these skeletons build up into the massive structures we call reefs.

The key to a reef's success is a partnership. Inside the tissues of most reef-building corals live microscopic algae. The algae use sunlight to produce food through photosynthesis, and they pass much of this food to the coral. In return, the coral provides the algae with shelter and with nutrients. The algae also give corals most of their colour. Because the algae need light, reef-building corals grow mainly in shallow, clear water in the tropics.

Although reefs cover well under one per cent of the ocean floor, they are home to roughly a quarter of all marine species. They also matter to people: they protect coastlines from waves and storms, support fishing, and attract tourists.

The greatest threat to reefs today is rising sea temperature. When the water becomes too warm for a long period, the partnership breaks down and the coral expels its algae. Without them, the coral turns white, which is why the process is called bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead, and if temperatures fall quickly it can recover, but if the heat continues, it may starve. In recent years, mass bleaching events have affected reefs around the world, including large parts of the Great Barrier Reef in Australia.

Other threats include pollution from farms, which carries fertiliser into coastal waters, and the increasing acidity of the ocean as it absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. More acidic water makes it harder for corals to build their skeletons.

What can be done? The most important action is to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, but scientists are also trying to help reefs directly. In coral gardening, small fragments of coral are grown in underwater nurseries and then planted back onto damaged reefs. Researchers are also studying corals that survive unusually warm water, in the hope of breeding more heat-tolerant varieties. These projects are promising, but they work on a small scale, and they cannot replace the need to protect reefs from warming in the first place.
That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
That is the end of the listening test.
